title: Oyster Bay: A Native Agreement and Expanding Colonial Claims
summary: Asiapum/Mohenes and three English purchasers are named in Oyster Bay’s 1653 agreement. Rivers, an excluded island, settler allotments and later boundary disputes reveal how colonial claims expanded across a Native landscape whose Matinecock connections continue.
address_label: Northern Nassau regional history — not a visitor entrance
map_geometry_source: Approximate regional reading area, not a deed survey. Historical river identifications, modern USGS flowlines, NYS Centre Island exclusion and project land mask; uncertain southern edge.
why_this_matters: A purchase date alone cannot explain the transfer of power. Named parties, excluded land, measured settler allotments and official recording show how a written claim worked, while Matinecock cultural work makes clear that the people did not disappear.

history_title: People, boundaries and the machinery of a land claim
history_content:
Finding this landscape

Oyster Bay harbor lies on Long Island's North Shore in present-day Nassau County. The much larger modern Town of Oyster Bay extends south to the bay shore facing the Atlantic. This account begins with a northern land agreement recorded in 1653; it does not treat the whole present town as one purchase or one moment of Native displacement. [1] Oyster Bay Town Records, volume I [2] The Early Settlement of Oyster Bay

Who made the 1653 agreement?

The surviving record names Asiapum, also written Mohenes, and three English purchasers: Peter Wright, Samuel Mayo and William Leverich. Its wording claims land between Oyster River on the east and Papaquatunk River on the west, extending toward a southern point of trees called Canteaiug. It includes woods, wetlands, ponds and offshore islands but specifically excludes Hog Island. The consideration included clothing, tools, kettles and wampum. [1] Oyster Bay Town Records, volume I

Hammond identifies Mohannes as a Matinecock sachem and places the agreement within English settlement from New England. The purchasers were operating amid competing Dutch and English claims to authority around the harbor. Those European claims are part of the colonial setting; they do not independently establish Native consent. [2] The Early Settlement of Oyster Bay

What the deed's language can—and cannot—tell us

The English text claims rights for the purchasers and their heirs, administrators and assigns. That language made the claim transferable beyond the people who met in 1653. A note on the reverse added other joint purchasers. A deed can therefore be followed as an instrument through which settlers claimed authority over fields, waterways and future generations' access. [1] Oyster Bay Town Records, volume I

The document records that claim; it is not a complete account of what every Native person understood, authorized or retained. Nor does it show that Native people lacked boundaries or land rights. Its own named rivers, tree-point and excluded island require us to take the geography seriously. Distinguishing the written colonial claim from all the relationships people maintained with land is essential to reading it responsibly. [1] Oyster Bay Town Records, volume I

From an agreement to settler allotments and official records

In 1663, the town appointed Nicholas Wright, Frances Weeks and Henry Townsend to lay out twenty acres for each eligible townsman who held a lot and commonage rights. The record shows a practical mechanism of settler control: town officials divided access to common land into measured allotments. It does not establish that all Native rights had ended. [6] Oyster Bay early documents: Commonage Rights, 1663

The earlier deed was entered in the New York office on March 27, 1667, by secretary Matthias Nicolls, and also in Oyster Bay’s book by John Newman. Recording gave the claim an enduring place in colonial administration. The 1667 endorsement is a recording date, not the date when the 1653 agreement was first made. [1] Oyster Bay Town Records, volume I

A Matinecock successor defines the bounds, 1678

On December 20, 1678, Suscaneman, also called Runasuck, described in the record as the chief proprietor of the Matinecock lands within Oyster Bay and successor to Asiopum, also called Mahams, set out the bounds of Asiopum's earlier sale. His line ran from the head of the Beaver Swamp River to the head of a stream called Suckscakes Wigwam, south to the line agreed with Robert Williams in 1664, to the head of Cold Spring, and north to the Sound. [1] Oyster Bay Town Records, volume I

The record shows Matinecock leadership passing from Asiopum to Suscaneman, and a Matinecock proprietor explaining, a generation later, what the first sale had included. It also notes that the town's freeholders protested the writing. [1] Oyster Bay Town Records, volume I

Six years later, on January 8, 1684, Suscaneman, "being Impowered by ye Indians to make Sale of matinecock Lands," promised in writing that as he received the pay he would distribute a part yearly to Tackapousha "and to Every Indian or Squaw Concernd." Payment for Matinecock land was owed to everyone who held a share in it. [1] Oyster Bay Town Records, volume I

An excluded island and an uncertain tree-point

Hog Island is present-day Centre Island. It should not be colored as part of this 1653 claim. Hammond identifies the eastern river with the stream at the head of Cold Spring Harbor and the western boundary with the Shu Swamp/Beaver system. These are historical geographic interpretations, not modern survey coordinates. [2] The Early Settlement of Oyster Bay

Cantiague presents a further caution. The New York State Museum's gazetteer distinguishes the early point of trees from the later boundary stone. The stone was moved to Cantiague Park in 1964. The same work cites Native testimony in 1698 identifying a marked white oak as the boundary location. The relocated monument cannot simply become an exact corner of this map. Native geographical knowledge continued to matter in later disputes. [3] Beyond Manhattan: CANTIAGUE

One agreement did not settle every claim

The Village of Matinecock's history describes a 1677 colonial boundary action by Governor Edmund Andros and a separate 1685 purchase north and west of the first tract. These later episodes must be mapped and explained individually. Extending the first deed's color across all of northern Nassau would conceal that sequence and erase the excluded land. [4] History of Matinecock

Matinecock history continues

Matinecock descendants continue public teaching, cultural work and family history across the North Shore. A 2018 Flushing Town Hall program brought together Donna Gentle Spirit Barron, Tecumseh Ceaser and Reggie Ceaser, whose biographies describe Matinecock and Montaukett family connections. These living relationships challenge any account that ends with the settlers' deed. This source does not establish a particular descendant's relationship to the named 1653 signatory, and this map does not presume one. [5] Honoring the First People of Queens

For the existing Historic Moment about the original agreement and its western river name, continue to Papequatunck.
whereintheworld_title: How to read this approximate map area
whereintheworld_content:
This is a regional reading area for the 1653 agreement and later colonial claims, not a surveyed deed footprint or present ownership map. It follows the interpreted Beaver Brook/Shu Swamp corridor on the west and Cold Spring Harbor/Brook on the east, using modern USGS waterways and the modern land mask. Inland connecting edges and the broad southern edge near the Cantiague/Jericho–Hicksville vicinity are interpretive: the original point of trees has not been georeferenced. The relocated stone at Cantiague Park is not used as an exact corner. Centre Island (Hog Island) is excluded using the modern NYS village outline with a small shoreline tolerance; other detached northern pieces and offshore islands are omitted pending separate research. This incomplete outline must not be read as every acre described in 1653, a single moment of removal, or the whole modern Town of Oyster Bay. Shores and streams have changed. It identifies no signing location, home, burial or archaeological site.

[2] The Early Settlement of Oyster Bay [3] Beyond Manhattan: CANTIAGUE [7] National Hydrography Dataset: modern flowlines [8] Charles T. Church (Shu Swamp) [9] NYS Civil Boundaries: Villages
